scope: Only actual supplier23 KL interface imports, transitive AC assumption, and concrete defect surfaced in required coordinate example. No broad ELBO/QMC audit or recursive unrelated supplier review.
supplier_statement:
Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$ \int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty, $$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$ \log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu). $$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.
supplier_proof:
1.1 If $P\not\ll Q$, [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$ but $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$, nonnegativity is immediate. It remains to consider $P\ll Q$ with finite divergence; let $r=dP/dQ$. [F1, given]

1.2 Put $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi(t)=t\log t$ for $t>0$. By [F5] and [F7], $\varphi''(t)=1/t>0$ for $t>0$, so [F8] makes $\varphi$ convex on $(0,\infty)$. Its continuity at zero is part of [F1]; taking limits in the convexity inequality as a positive endpoint tends to zero extends convexity to $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

1.3 Define $g(t):=t\log t-t+1$ for $t>0$ and $g(0):=1$. For $s>1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=\int_1^cdu/u+\int_c^sdu/u$. On $[1,c]$, $1/u\le1$, while on $[c,s]$, $1/u\le1/c<1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. For $0<s<1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=-\int_s^1du/u=-\left(\int_s^cdu/u+\int_c^1du/u\right)$. On $[s,c]$, $1/u\ge1/c>1$, and on $[c,1]$, $1/u\ge1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. The integrands and comparison constants are integrable on these compact intervals by [F10]. Equality holds at $s=1$. Applying this inequality to $s=1/t$ and using [F6] gives $t\log t\ge t-1$, strictly unless $t=1$. Hence $g\ge0$ and its only zero is $1$. [F4, F6, F9, F10, F11, F24, algebra]

1.4 For the normalized-density clause on the measure space [F13], put $P:=q\,\mu$ and $Q:=\pi\,\mu$. By [F17], $\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1$; hence [F15] and [F14] make $P$ and $Q$ probability measures. [F13, F14, F15, F17, given, algebra]

1.5 If $Q(E)=0$, [F15] gives $\int_E\pi\,d\mu=0$, hence $\int_E\gamma\,d\mu=0$ because $Z$ is finite and positive, using [F17]. By [F12], $\gamma=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $E$. The support hypothesis on $q$ then gives $P(E)=0$, so $P\ll Q$. Define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These are Borel by [F18], so [F19] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F20]–[F21], $r:=q\,\rho(\pi)$ is measurable and equals $q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and zero on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $E$, [F16] gives $$ \int_E r\,dQ=\int_Er\pi\,d\mu=\int_Eq\,d\mu=P(E), $$ because $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. Thus $r=dP/dQ$. [F12, F15, F16, F17, F18, F19, F20, F21, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] with $E$ equal to the whole space, $\int r\,dQ=P(\Omega)=1$. The negative part of $r\log r$ is finite by [F1], so finiteness of $D(P\|Q)$ also makes its positive part finite. Thus $r$ and $r\log r$ are integrable with respect to the probability measure $Q$. The Radon–Nikodym representative here is the one whose selection is covered by [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 On the $P$-full-measure subset of $\{q>0\}$ where $\gamma>0$, we have $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\ell:=\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. Where $q=0$, the KL logarithm $\ell$ is defined to be zero. By [F23], $q|\ell|\le q|\log q|+q|\log\gamma|+q|\log Z|$ almost everywhere. The right-hand side has finite integral by the hypotheses and $\int q=1$; hence [F16] gives $\int|\ell|\,dP=\int q|\ell|\,d\mu<\infty$. By [F1], [F16], and [F22], applying [F16] to the positive and negative parts of $\ell$ gives $$ D(P\|Q)=\int\log r\,dP =\int q(\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z)\,d\mu. $$ Using $\int q\,d\mu=1$ and rearranging proves the identity. [A1, F1, F16, F22, F23, given, step 1.5, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ to $r$ and $\varphi$. Steps 2.1 and 1.2 check its integrability and convexity hypotheses, and $\int r\,dQ=1$ by step 2.1. Therefore $$ 0=\varphi(1)=\varphi\!\left(\int r\,dQ\right) \le\int\varphi(r)\,dQ=D(P\|Q). $$ [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2]

3.2 Since $\int r\,dQ=\int1\,dQ=1$, we have $D(P\|Q)=\int g(r)\,dQ$. If $D(P\|Q)=0$, [F12] gives $g(r)=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere, so $r=1$ $Q$-almost everywhere. The Radon–Nikodym identity [F2] then gives $P(E)=Q(E)$ for every measurable $E$. Conversely, if $P=Q$ then $r=1$ almost everywhere and [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, F12, step 2.1, step 1.3, algebra]

4.1 Step 2.2 identifies the normalized-density divergence as finite, and step 3.1 proves it is nonnegative. Therefore $\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu\le\log Z$, as claimed. [step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$, write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use $0\log0=0$, and set the products $q\log\gamma$ and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

Let $\mu,\gamma,Z,\pi,q$ satisfy [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]], and put $Q=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi=\pi\,\mu$. The choice-free density-ratio identity
$$\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$$
holds, with the ratio integrand set to zero where $q=0$. Under AC, the final integral is the library reverse divergence $D(Q\|\Pi)$ and is nonnegative. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z.$$
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Define $Q(A)=\int_A q\,d\mu$ and $\Pi(A)=\int_A\pi\,d\mu$. These are probability measures by [F1] and [F7]. If $\Pi(A)=0$, [F4] applied to $\pi\mathbf1_A$ gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. Then [F1] gives $q=0$ almost everywhere on $A$, so $Q(A)=0$ and $Q\ll\Pi$. Define $r=q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and $r=0$ on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $A$, $\int_A r\,d\Pi=\int_{A\cap\{\pi>0\}}q\,d\mu=Q(A)$, so $r=dQ/d\Pi$. [F1, F4, F7, construct, algebra]

2.1 On $\{q>0\}$, $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. The assumed absolute integrability and $\int q\,d\mu=1$ make all terms integrable. Hence $\int\log r\,dQ=\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu=\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)$. This algebraic identity uses the explicit density ratio and no choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [A1] and [F5], the integral $\int\log r\,dQ$ is $D(Q\|\Pi)$ under the library convention. Rearranging step 2.1 gives $\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+D(Q\|\Pi)$. [A1, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The measures $Q$ and $\Pi$ are probabilities, so [F6] gives $D(Q\|\Pi)\ge0$. Step 3.1 then yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z$. [F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface:
**Inputs:** A finite number $m\ge1$ of sigma-finite factor reference spaces $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$, their product reference measure $\mu$, a measurable target $\gamma$ with finite positive normalizer, an admissible initial mean-field density $q=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j$, and a finite sweep count $N\ge0$.

**Output:** The current admissible product density after at most $N$ full sweeps, together with a status indicating whether the requested sweeps completed or a coordinate update was unavailable.

For each sweep $t=1,\ldots,N$, visit coordinates in the fixed order $j=1,\ldots,m$. At coordinate $j$, keep $q_{-j}:=\prod_{k\ne j}q_k$ fixed; for $m=1$, the empty product reference space is a singleton with unit measure $\mu_{-j}$ and its density is $1$. Form the conditional log expectation
$$h_j(z_j):=\int_{\prod_{k\ne j}\Omega_k}\log\gamma(z_j,z_{-j})q_{-j}(z_{-j})\,d\mu_{-j}(z_{-j}).$$
Use this signed integral only when it is defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity and has a measurable extended-real version; require it to be finite for current $q_j$-almost every $z_j$. Set
$$c_j:=\int_{\Omega_j}e^{h_j(z_j)}\,\mu_j(dz_j).$$
If $0<c_j<\infty$ and the normalized density $q_j^*(z_j):=e^{h_j(z_j)}/c_j$ makes $q_j^*q_{-j}$ an admissible member of the mean-field family, replace $q_j$ by $q_j^*$. Otherwise stop and return the current density with status “coordinate update unavailable.”

The algorithm performs only the requested finite sweeps. It makes no convergence, stationary-point, global-optimum, calibration, or approximation-error claim. A separate theorem on this page proves exact coordinate monotonicity under these conditions.
The claim that maximizing the ELBO over independent Gaussian factors always recovers the target's marginal variances is false, even for a nonsingular centered bivariate Gaussian target.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The hypotheses and explicit densities in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $s=\sqrt\beta$ and $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. Rescaling $t$ by $\sqrt2$ in [F3] gives $\int\phi=1$. The target factors as $\gamma_\rho(x,y)=\phi(x)s^{-1}\phi((y-\rho x)/s)$; the substitution $u=(y-\rho x)/s$ gives $\int s^{-1}\phi((y-\rho x)/s)dy=1$. Tonelli [F4] therefore shows $\gamma_\rho$ integrates to one and has $x$-marginal $\phi$. Completing the square gives $\gamma_\rho(x,y)=\phi(y)s^{-1}\phi((x-\rho y)/s)$, so the $y$-marginal is also $\phi$. Integration by parts using $\phi'(t)=-t\phi(t)$ and $t\phi(t)\to0$ at both tails gives $\int t^2\phi(t)dt=1$; hence both target marginal variances equal $1$. Since $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$, the cross moment is absolutely integrable. Fubini gives $E[XY]=\int x\phi(x)(\rho x)dx=\rho$, because the conditional $y$ factor has mean $\rho x$ by the oddness of $t\phi(t)$. Thus the covariance is $\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$. [given, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For $m_j\in\mathbb R$ and $v_j>0$, rescaling the same Gaussian integral [F3] shows $g_{m_j,v_j}$ integrates to one. Direct integration by parts gives its mean $m_j$ and variance $v_j$: after $z=m_j+\sqrt{v_j}t$, the odd integral $\int t\phi(t)dt$ is zero and $\int t^2\phi(t)dt=1$ by step 1.1. Its log density and $\log\gamma_\rho$ are quadratic. The second moments above and $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ make the cross term integrable; the quadratic log terms are therefore integrable and the product $q$ satisfies [F1]. Fubini [F5] and the product-density identity [F6] give $E_q[X^2]=m_1^2+v_1$, $E_q[Y^2]=m_2^2+v_2$, and $E_q[XY]=m_1m_2$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 From the displayed density, $\log\gamma_\rho=-\log(2\pi s)-(x^2-2\rho xy+y^2)/(2\beta)$. Also $-E_{g_{m_j,v_j}}\log g_{m_j,v_j}=\tfrac12\log(2\pi v_j)+\tfrac12$, by the moments in step 2.1. Substituting these expectations into [F2] gives
$\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=C_\rho-\frac{m_1^2-2\rho m_1m_2+m_2^2+v_1+v_2}{2\beta}+\frac12\log v_1+\frac12\log v_2$, where $C_\rho$ is independent of $m_1,m_2,v_1,v_2$. The mean quadratic equals $(m_1-\rho m_2)^2+\beta m_2^2$, so its unique minimizing, hence ELBO-maximizing, means are $m_1=m_2=0$. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each variance, the part depending on $v$ is $g(v)=-v/(2\beta)+(1/2)\log v$. Its derivative is $g'(v)=(\beta-v)/(2\beta v)$, positive for $0<v<\beta$ and negative for $v>\beta$. Thus the unique maximizer is $v=\beta$. Since $0<|\rho|<1$, $0<\beta<1$, proving strict variance underestimation. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface: Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-coordinate-ascent-variational-inference]]. At a coordinate $j$, suppose the conditional expectation $h_j$ has the stated finite-valued version, $0<c_j=\int e^{h_j}d\mu_j<\infty$, and $q_j^*q_{-j}$ is admissible. Then $q_j^*=e^{h_j}/c_j$ attains the maximum of $\operatorname{ELBO}(r_jq_{-j})$ over all admissible coordinate replacements $r_j$. In particular, replacing the current factor by $q_j^*$ does not decrease the ELBO. This is a single-update claim; it gives no convergence or global-optimum conclusion.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix any admissible replacement $r_j$ and form $u=r_jq_{-j}$. Tonelli [F5] gives $\int u\,d\mu=1$, and the product rectangle formula [F4] gives $\mathbb P_u:=u\mu=\bigotimes_{k=1}^m(u_k\mu_k)$ is the product probability. Each coordinate density $u_k$ is positive and finite almost surely under its factor law; put $X_k=\log u_k(Z_k)$ and $S=\log u(Z)=\sum_{k=1}^mX_k$. By [F1], $\mathbb E_u|S|=\int u|\log u|d\mu<\infty$. Fix $j$ and put $R=\sum_{k\ne j}X_k$, which is finite almost surely under the product of the other factor laws. Since $\{|R|\le n\}$ increases to a full-measure set, choose an integer $K$ for which $p:=\mathbb P_u(|R|\le K)>0$. Product integration from [F5] and [F6] then gives $p\int u_j|\log u_j|d\mu_j=\int_{\{|R|\le K\}}|X_j|\,d\mathbb P_u\le\int|S|d\mathbb P_u+Kp<\infty$, using $|X_j|\le|S|+|R|$ on that event. Thus every factor log is integrable; the same argument applies to the current factor and to $q_j^*$ because their products are admissible. [F1, F4, F5, F6, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 For each admissible replacement $u_j$, [F1] makes $u\log\gamma$ absolutely integrable. Fubini [F7] applies also to $u|\log\gamma|$, so $\int u_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$ and exchanging the $j$ and $-j$ integrals gives $\int u\log\gamma d\mu=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j$. By step 1.1, all factor log terms are integrable, so $\log u=\log u_j+\log q_{-j}$ almost surely and $\operatorname{ELBO}(u_jq_{-j})=\int u_jh_jd\mu_j-\int u_j\log u_jd\mu_j-\int q_{-j}\log q_{-j}d\mu_{-j}$. The final term is constant over coordinate replacements. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $q_j^*=e^{h_j}/c_j$. If $q_j^*=0$, then $h_j=-\infty$ almost everywhere on that set. For any admissible $r_j$, step 2.1 makes $\int r_j|h_j|d\mu_j<\infty$, hence $r_j=0$ almost everywhere there. Thus $r_j\mu_j\ll q_j^*\mu_j$. On $\{q_j^*>0\}$ the ratio $r_j/q_j^*$ is measurable, and for every measurable $A$, $\int_A(r_j/q_j^*)d(q_j^*\mu_j)=\int_{A\cap\{q_j^*>0\}}r_jd\mu_j=\int_Ar_jd\mu_j$, so it is the Radon–Nikodym density. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 By [A1] and [F8], $D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)=\int r_j\log(r_j/q_j^*)d\mu_j=\int r_j\log r_jd\mu_j-\int r_jh_jd\mu_j+\log c_j$. All terms are finite by step 1.1 and step 2.1. Also $\int q_j^*h_j-\int q_j^*\log q_j^*=\log c_j$. Subtracting the ELBO expressions in step 2.1 therefore gives $\operatorname{ELBO}(q_j^*q_{-j})-\operatorname{ELBO}(r_jq_{-j})=D(r_j\mu_j\|q_j^*\mu_j)\ge0$ by [F9]. Hence $q_j^*$ is an attained exact coordinate maximizer. [A1, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The current factor $q_j$ is itself an admissible replacement. Taking $r_j=q_j$ in step 3.2 proves that the update does not decrease ELBO. [step 3.2, given] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface: The numerical value of an ELBO depends on the scale of the unnormalized target. It alone is not a bound on posterior discrepancy, calibration, or downstream error. Here a calibration guarantee means a separately proved property of repeated-sampling coverage or posterior-probability calibration; it is not defined by the ELBO. The exact identity controls the gap $\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)$ through the reverse divergence, when that gap is known.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix any $c\in\mathbb R$. By the onto clause of [F5], choose $a>0$ with $\log a=c$. Define $\gamma_c=a\gamma$. Homogeneity [F4] gives $Z_c=\int\gamma_c d\mu=aZ$, so $\pi_c=\gamma_c/Z_c=\pi$ and both $Q$ and $\Pi$ remain unchanged. Since $\pi_c=\pi$, the support condition in [F1] is unchanged. On the q-support, $|\log\gamma_c|\le|\log\gamma|+|c|$, so the logarithmic integrability condition remains finite. [F1, F4, F5, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 On the q-support the logarithm product law [F5] gives $\log\gamma_c=\log\gamma+c$. Using [F2], $\operatorname{ELBO}_c(q)=\int q(\log\gamma+c-\log q)d\mu=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+c$. Since $c$ is arbitrary, the absolute ELBO can be made arbitrarily large while $Q$, $\Pi$, and any fixed discrepancy between them stay unchanged. [F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The decomposition [F3] gives $\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=D(Q\|\Pi)$. Without control of $\log Z$, a separate calibration theorem, or another posterior-discrepancy bound, the absolute ELBO alone supplies no calibration guarantee. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface: Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}$ with counting measure, $\gamma(0)=2$, and $\gamma(1)=1$. Then $Z=3$ and $\pi=(2/3,1/3)$. Taking $q=\pi$ attains $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=\log3$. The distinct admissible density $q=(1/2,1/2)$ gives $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=\tfrac32\log2<\log3$.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The data in the Example.

1.1 Counting measure gives $Z=2+1=3$ and $\pi=(2/3,1/3)$. For $q=\pi$, each positive coordinate has $\log q(x)=\log\gamma(x)-\log3$, so the defining sum is $\operatorname{ELBO}(\pi)=\log3$. Both terms are finite and $q$ is supported on $\pi$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For $q=(1/2,1/2)$, the defining sum is $\tfrac12\log2+\log2=\tfrac32\log2$. Since $(2^{3/2})^2=8<9=3^2$ and both bases are positive, $2^{3/2}<3$. The log laws give $\log3-\tfrac32\log2=\tfrac12\log(9/8)>0$, because $9/8>1$ and [F2] makes $\log$ strictly increasing with $\log1=0$. This density is admissible because both target weights are positive and the space is finite. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface: On $\Omega=\{0,1\}$ with counting measure, take $\gamma=(1,0)$. Then $Z=1$ and $\pi=(1,0)$. The probability density $q=(0,1)$ is supported entirely outside the target support, so it is not admissible and has no finite ELBO.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** The data in the Example.

1.1 Counting measure gives $Z=1$ and $\pi=(1,0)$. At the point $1$, $q(1)=1$ but $\pi(1)=0$, so the support condition in [F1] fails. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Also $\gamma(1)=0$ and $q(1)=1$, so $q(1)|\log\gamma(1)|=+\infty$. The absolute-integrability condition in [F1] fails as well; the finite-ELBO identity is not applicable to this candidate. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

consumer_dispositions.exact_interface: There are a finite-evidence target $\gamma$ and an admissible product density $q$ for which the expected-log coordinate function is identically zero on a countably infinite counting space. Its exponential therefore has infinite normalizer, so the coordinate update is unavailable.
consumer_dispositions.exact_argument:
**Given:** Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$, let $\mu_X$ be counting measure, and let $\mu_Y(\{m\})=w_m$ be the atomic measure defined below.

1.1 Put $r_n=2^{-n}$, $b_n=-2\log(n+1)$, $a_n=-(1-r_n)b_n/r_n=2(2^n-1)\log(n+1)>0$, and $w_m=e^{-2a_m}$. Define $\gamma(n,m)=e^{a_n}$ when $m=n$ and $\gamma(n,m)=e^{b_n}=(n+1)^{-2}$ otherwise. By [F3],
$Z=\sum_m e^{-2a_m}\left(e^{a_m}+\sum_{n\ne m}(n+1)^{-2}\right)$. For every $m$, $a_m\ge2\log(m+1)>0$, so $e^{-a_m}\le(m+1)^{-2}$. Also $\sum_n(n+1)^{-2}<\infty$ because $(n+1)^{-2}\le[n(n+1)]^{-1}=1/n-1/(n+1)$. Hence $0<Z\le\sum_m e^{-a_m}+\left(\sum_m e^{-2a_m}\right)\left(\sum_n(n+1)^{-2}\right)<\infty$. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Give the $X$-factor masses $q_X(n)=r_n$ and the $Y$-factor density $q_Y(m)=r_m/w_m$ relative to $\mu_Y$. Each factor has total mass $\sum_n r_n=1$, so $q(n,m)=r_nr_m/w_m$ is a product probability density by [F3]. It is positive wherever $\gamma$ is positive, so it satisfies the support condition in [F1]. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For fixed $n$, the expectation of $\log\gamma(n,Y)$ under $q_Y$ is $r_na_n+(1-r_n)b_n=0$. Its absolute expectation is $r_na_n+(1-r_n)|b_n|=2(1-r_n)|b_n|\le4\log(n+1)$. Therefore $\int q|\log\gamma|d\mu\le4\sum_n2^{-n}\log(n+1)<\infty$. For $n\ge1$, [F4] and [F5] give $\log(n+1)=\int_1^{n+1}dt/t\le n$, since $0<1/t\le1$ on $[1,n+1]$. Also, for $n\ge4$ one has $n\le2^{n/2}$ by induction, so $n2^{-n}\le2^{-n/2}$ and the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $\log q(n,m)=-n\log2-m\log2+2a_m$, the triangle inequality gives $\int q|\log q|d\mu\le2\log2\sum_n n2^{-n}+2\sum_m2^{-m}a_m$. The first series is finite by the same geometric bound as in step 3.1, and $2^{-m}a_m=2(1-2^{-m})\log(m+1)\le2\log(m+1)$ makes the second finite by that bound. Thus [F1] holds and $q$ is admissible. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the $X$-coordinate update with $q_Y$ fixed, step 3.1 gives $h(n)=E_{q_Y}\log\gamma(n,Y)=0$ for every $n$. Therefore the update normalizer in [F2] is $\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{h(n)}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty1=\infty$. The expected log is finite and the current product is admissible, but no normalized coordinate factor exists. [F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
